Wilhelm Wackernagel, writing in 1838, says that the source of tragedy is historical reality belonging to the past. Present reality, by contrast, belongs to comedy and is the source of the comic!
Is this difference simply the result of the contrast between today and the respectable Biedermeier Basel of his time?
In any case, the distinction is very sharply drawn and deserves further thought.
In my assessment of Adolf Grabowsky’s essay on myth, there is this sentence:
A glissando of quotations, as though straight out of a card index; everything has been put to use, nothing has been worked through.
Who hears everything contained in that sentence?
Who recognizes that an entire type is being disposed of there?
More generally, who does this description fit: putting things to use without working them through?
And what personal passion of mine lies behind it?
Probably the Hegelian struggle between master and servant.
Putting something to use without working it through—is that pure consumption?
Now, once again, I find myself hunting for a person. I want at any price to meet Pierre Leyris, a French author whose short essay on Benito Cereno I read in Spanish.
The Spanish essay appeared in 1944 as an afterword to a Chilean edition of Melville’s story, in a cheap series of novellas and tales.
Pierre Leyris says that every detail in Melville’s story has a double meaning, and that every reader can find his own path through this bottomless book.
The American literary historians noticed nothing of this, although they did establish the differences between old Amasa Delano’s original report and Melville’s story.
Melville keeps opening up new abysses against his own will. He does not speak about the problem of the slave trade.

According to Leyris, he turns the slave ship into the condition of original sin: the slave trade itself is original sin. And the American has fallen under original sin not so deeply, but only weakly—debilmente.
That was not allowed to happen.
Benito leaps from the Navío de las Penas, the Ship of Sorrows, into the little boat of redemption.
Melville’s Benito Cereno should have had the subtitle:
And so Pierre Leyris’s marvelous starting point runs aground in the abstract banality of scholastic theology and all its endless talk.
These Black men killed the heir, poor Don Alejandro. Once the heir has been killed, both inheritance and property come to an end.
Who, then, are these vineyard tenants in Matthew 21?
After the workers in the vineyard in chapter 20, who demand a fair wage, come the vineyard tenants of chapter 21, who kill the vineyard owner’s heir.
A beautiful subject for a song by Bert Brecht, with a fiery final effect: the heir is beaten to death; the leap into the realm of freedom has been made.

Sigmund Freud still knew what it meant that they had killed the prophets—even Moses himself. He therefore understood more about Christianity than the whole Thomist tradition of the celibate bureaucracy, which deprives precisely this—the killing of the heir—of its concrete presence and thereby becomes an accomplice.
Hamann and Bruno Bauer understood this.
This is the end of the Christian age.
Luther was the great katechon, the great restrainer.
Nietzsche’s rage against Luther and Hegel was justified from Nietzsche’s own point of view.
Hegel too was a great katechon.
The great German emperors were katechontes. Hence the hatred of Hegel—a hatred that would otherwise be impossible to explain.
Bring me my writing tablets! Bring me my notebook!
A beautiful title for a diary.
And what drives Hamlet to make his note?
The discovery of a villain—a villain who smiles. These are the human things worth thinking about and worth writing down. These are what fill the tables.

This My tables! came to me early this morning, at dawn, when I finally understood what happened to me in May 1953 at Herrenalb and Baden-Baden: the insulting way I was thrown out, and the removal of my lecture on the κατέχων, so that Gerhard Günther could take over the subject.

Schomerus now celebrates that conference in the Linksrheinischer Merkur of 23 September 1955 as his finest conference, precisely because of Gerhard Günther’s lecture—which was in truth nothing more than an unoriginal repetition of the views of his brother Albrecht Erich.
I wanted to carry Albrecht Erich’s thought further.
That was precisely what had to be prevented.
How slow I am to catch on!
How good-heartedly stupid—and stupidly good-hearted—I am!
It took that article in the Linksrheinischer Merkur. But that article makes it clear.
Who is so stupid he cannot see the fraud? And who so bold as to say that he sees it?
Again and again I have fallen for the fraud.
Schiller’s Marianism is a subject that could be treated together with Hegel’s Marianism.
The outburst of the exposed traitor Mortimer in Mary Stuart, Act IV, Scene 4, at the end—“Mary, holy one, pray for me”—has too much overwhelming force to have been merely invented.
What did these Swabians still have inside them?
And how much did they still know?
Goethe’s Marianism has no martial drive.
In Schiller it becomes a conquering Conquista.

The earthly Mary and the heavenly Mary flow into one another. For 155 years Germans have been watching and listening to this scene, and no one dares to think about what is being revealed to them there.
Perhaps it will become clear to us on Schiller’s 200th birthday in 1959.

According to Friedrich Glum (Mirror and Distorting Mirror of the Philosophers), Christianity is indispensable to democracy—though only secularized Christianity, of course, a Christianity in which both Christians and non-Christians can make themselves at home!
Or Rüdiger Altmann, in Civis, November 1955: in reality, he says, there is no material ethic in the Western cultural world today other than the Christian one.

And it dares to quote Kierkegaard instead of being honest and beating him to death, as he himself demanded. But even this preacher of repentance, who declared being beaten to death to be the test of whether a preacher of repentance was genuine—even this Christian who called for himself to be beaten to death—disappeared into the universal irony.

People only applauded him all the more enthusiastically. When a serious individual enters into a race with the public in an atmosphere where every ideology has been swallowed by total irony, that poor individual must eventually collapse from sheer exhaustion and die—naturally to the applause of the very same public he thought he was spitting in the face.

Thanks to the angel who grabbed me by the hair and set me down outside this Christian cultural establishment; who knocked this cup of the murkiest poison out of my hand before it reached my lips; and who showed me the spring from which I am allowed to drink: the spring of poverty and freedom.
So first there is the little man, the μικρός ἄνθρωπος, the parvus homo. That is me, for example. And that is you.
Then there is the great man, the magnus homo. That is, for example, the USA or the USSR as directly great powers—or the Pope as an indirectly great power.
In short, the question arises: what do you, little man, still want at all?
What makes you think that, being little, you have any right to speak about someone great?
The great man has no time for you!
Do you want to become a nuisance to him?
Do you want to disturb the intrigues of his antechamber lackeys?
You, being little, have only little worries.
The great ones, however—Mr. Stalin, for example, or Hitler, or the Holy Father—have only great worries.

Woe to you if one of them should ever get the idea of noticing you at all, in order to prove to himself, to the world, and to democracy that the little people too are equal to the great and enjoy the interest of the great. Then you will discover the connection between protection and obedience. And every other great power, which you can no longer obey, will become your enemy.

“The Christian today, if he still wishes to be called a Christian, must bind himself in the strictest possible way to the original Christian ethic,” Karl Korn said in 1948, in the Berliner Hefte, in his essay “Kyklos.”
Compare this with what Glum and Altmann say above, under 6 November 1955.
Is a person not supposed to go mad listening to all this talk about Christianity?
To one it is ethos, to another it is value; The whole thing is not worth a single shot of powder.
But one can make a living from that too. It is even a reliable protection against the shot of powder—or against the atom bomb.
The shamelessness with which people now, in November 1955, talk about Kierkegaard in newspapers and on the radio overwhelms any remaining thought that mutual understanding might still be possible.
You would have no right to be surprised or even to complain—and you do neither.
